II): the English column reads “Just as iron rusts unless it is used, and water putrifies or, in cold, turns to ice, so our intellect spoils unless it is kept in use.”, directly after the Mount Etna sentence, facing the Italian “Siccome il ferro s’arruginiscie sanza esercitio…”. The spelling putrifies is the 1883 edition’s (the same volume spells putrefy elsewhere, so it is an inconsistency in the book, not a transcription slip). Gutenberg numbers the group 1177 and the preface credits the translation mainly to Mrs R. C. Bell, as the source says. This is the honest wording: the version that circulates (“Iron rusts from disuse; stagnant water loses its purity…”) is a later and freer rendering, and the line ships in Richter’s text, not that one. shipped.js: not shipped, no near line, Leonardo at 0, not banned.
